ABSTRACT
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare dis-
order that affects the central nervous sys-
tem, being characterized by intermittent
episodes of muscle spasms, rigidity, and
a significant increase in morbidity and
mortality, We report a 29-year-old patient,
with left-sided chylothorax and thymoma,
who presented with truncal, lower ex-
tremities stiffness and painful cramps al-
leviated by diazepam and opiates. His
clinical picture was suggestive of SPS sec-
ondary to invasive thymoma. This syn-
drome is best approached by its early
recognition and prompt treatment since a
missed diagnosis can have deleterious
outcome. An intensive search for the un-
derlying etiology is of utmost importance
in the management of SPS. A review of the
current literature is also included in this
manuscript.

CASE PRESENTATION
A 29-year-old previously healthy African-
American male patient complained of
four-week history of progressive shortness
of breath, non-productive cough and left-
sided chest pain. Chest radiograph re-
vealed complete opacification of the left
hemithorax with shift of the mediastinum
to the right (Figure 1). Computed tomog-
raphy of the chest demonstrated a large
left-sided pleural effusion and a large an-
terior mediastinal mass (Figure 2). The
patient underwent a left thoracocentesis.
Fluid analysis was suggestive of chylotho-
rax (milky appearance, triglycerides 1845
mg/dl with normal serum triglycerides,

Cholesterol 27 mg/dl). PET scan
showed anterior mediastinal mass
with no significant increased activ-
ity. Laboratory data including blood,
urine, AFB’s were normal. Patient
underwent an open biopsy of the an-
terior mediastinal mass with the re-
sultant pathology specimen being
consistent with lymphocytic pre-
dominant epithelial type thymoma.
Due to the invasive behavior of this
neoplasm, an initial surgical treat-
ment was deferred and patient was
discharged home to be started on
four-drug-regimen chemotherapy
(Adriamycin, Cisplatin, Vincristine,
Cyclophosphamide) every three
weeks on an outpatient basis. Sev-
enty-two hours after discharge and
before receiving any chemotherapy,
the patient started having severe bi-
lateral lower extremity pain, muscle
cramps and weakness in both legs.
The patient did not have any short-
ness of breath, change in his bowel
habits, headache, double vision, dys-
phagia or other neurologic symp-
toms. Repeated physical
examination revealed evidence of an
unsteady antalgic gait, diffuse mus-
cular stiffness in both lower extrem-
ities along with diffuse lower back
pain. The rest of the neurologic ex-
amination was normal. Patient was
given diazepam 5 mg intravenously
along with intravenous morphine
with complete resolution of his
symptoms. In order to rule out other
associated disorders a full labora-
tory workup was done including a
paraneoplastic panel which included
anti-GAD antibodies; the result was
negative. Myasthenia gravis was
ruled out by a normal pulmonary
function test and a negative anti-
AChR antibodies test. Based on the
clinical picture, excluding other eti-
ologies, and the dramatic response
to benzodiazepine and opiates, the
diagnosis of SPS was made. Patient
received chemotherapy as planned
and at five-month follow up he did-
n’t have any recurrence of his symp-
toms with complete radiographic

resolution of his thymoma, which re-
sponded well to the chemotherapy.

In our patient, sur-
gical therapy was not an option because

of the aggressive behavior of the thymoma

invading surrounding structures, and the
decision was to opt for a chemotherapy
trial with good clinical and radiographic
outcome.

In our
patient the early recognition and treat-
ment management led to rapid recovery.
